analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 tax cuts permanent by removing their scheduled expiration.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors and was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, died there without ever getting a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) included an expiration date, meaning its tax cuts were set to end after 2010. This bill would erase that expiration date, making every provision of the 2001 law permanent — including lower income tax rates, the estate tax phase-out, expanded child and education credits, and the earned income tax credit expansion. It was introduced by a single representative, attracted no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most if the bill passes, because the largest provisions of the 2001 law — lower top rates, the estate tax repeal, and lower taxes on investment income — flow overwhelmingly to them [S2][S3]. Middle-income families also gain from permanent child tax credits, the earned income tax credit expansion, and education savings provisions [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High-income households, plus families with children

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the expiration date of the 2001 tax law so its provisions no longer end automatically [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the law's income tax cuts, estate tax repeal, and gift tax changes [S2][S3].
Makes permanent the law's expansions of the earned income tax credit, child care and education benefits, and education savings accounts, which the bill's subject list covers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passes, the federal government collects less revenue every year, permanently, and the shortfall shows up as larger deficits or as cuts to other programs. Because the biggest tax cuts go to high-income households, the net effect shifts the burden toward everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal revenue, ultimately taxpayers and program funding

drawbacks.text: Permanently locking in the 2001 tax cuts removes the scheduled 2011 expiration that was originally included to limit the law's ten-year cost, so the full revenue loss recurs every year going forward [S2][S3].

The benefits of the 2001 law are concentrated at the top of the income scale — lower top rates, capital gains relief, and the estate tax phase-out — so making it permanent directs the largest permanent gains to the wealthiest households while the cost is spread across all federal taxpayers and future program budgets [S2][S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that making the cuts permanent means finding roughly $1 trillion-plus in offsetting savings or accepting larger deficits; the bill provides no offsets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real middle-class benefit here — permanent child credits, the EITC expansion, and education provisions help ordinary families [S2]. But the distribution of the 2001 tax cuts skews heavily toward high-income households and estates, and this bill would make that distribution permanent with no offsetting revenue, so the fiscal cost falls on future budgets. On balance the bill's main effect is a large, permanent transfer toward the wealthiest households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and nothing ever happened to it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Jo Bonner introduced the bill on January 28, 2003, the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
No further action was taken; the bill sat in committee until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the scheduled expiration of the 2001 tax cuts stayed on the books, preserving future federal revenue that a permanent extension would have given up. The people who would have gained the most — high-income households facing the estate tax phase-out — had to pursue the question in later legislation, and the single sponsor gained nothing from the effort. Low- and middle-income families who would have kept the EITC and child credit expansions gained nothing either, though they also avoided the deficit consequences.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue; scheduled expirations stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Jo Bonner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the sunset of the 2001 tax cuts; it drew no cosponsors and no committee action

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it died there

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and never reached a vote, so no party alignment can be measured from the record.

industries.note: Making the 2001 law permanent would lock in the provisions that benefit them most: lower top rates, capital gains relief, and the estate tax phase-out. Their gain is a permanent reduction in federal revenue that would otherwise be available for public programs or deficit reduction.

The same law included the expanded earned income tax credit, child credits, and education savings provisions that expire on the same schedule; making them permanent helps ordinary families. This benefit is real but is the smaller share of the law's total cost.
